title: SEED Labs - DNS Rebinding Attack Lab
description: Circumvent the browser Same-Origin Policy (SOP) using DNS Rebinding to attack protected IoT devices behind firewalls.
prerequisites: Basic Linux CLI and networking commands (dig, curl, ip)
Familiarity with DNS resolution, BIND9, and TTL mechanics
Understanding of the browser Same-Origin Policy (SOP) and JavaScript AJAX
outcomes: Understand DNS architecture, authoritative nameservers, forwarders, and caching mechanisms.
Analyze how browsers enforce the Same-Origin Policy (SOP) on web applications.
Perform manual DNS Rebinding by manipulating BIND9 zone files, TTL values, and browser DNS caching.
Execute an automated DNS Rebinding attack against an internal IoT smart thermostat.

levels.title: Introduction to DNS Rebinding
levels.content:
# SEED Labs – DNS Rebinding Attack Lab

### Objective & Scenario
Many Internet of Things (IoT) devices have simple built-in web servers for local configuration and control. Typically, these devices are placed behind private home/office firewalls, unreachable from the outside internet. Because they are shielded by the firewall, many IoT devices do not implement strong authentication mechanisms.

In this lab, the target is a **smart thermostat** located inside a protected internal network. Outside attackers cannot directly access this IoT device from the internet.

To compromise the IoT device, the attacker gets an internal user to visit a malicious website hosting attacker-controlled JavaScript. Although the script runs inside the user's browser behind the firewall, the browser's **Same-Origin Policy (SOP)** sandbox prevents the attacker's script from sending requests to the IoT device's origin.

The objective of this lab is to use the **DNS Rebinding** technique to circumvent this sandbox protection, extract the anti-CSRF secret password from the IoT thermostat, and change the room temperature to dangerously high values.

### General Rules & Anti-Cheating Protection
* Each student works in an isolated sandbox with **dynamically generated flags**. Sharing flags will not work.
* Total grading is on **20/20 points**.
* Using hints incurs a penalty between **-0.5 and -2.0 points**.

levels.title: Access the Sandbox
levels.cloud_content:
Your first task is to access the sandbox environment. When ready, submit the passkey **`start`**.

### Sandbox Access:
1. In the topology overview on the right, right-click on **`attacker`** and click **`Open GUI`** (or connect via SSH).
2. Login with username **`user`** and password **`Password123`** (or username **`seed`** / password **`dees`**).
3. You also have access to the **`victim-iot`** machine to observe the victim's browser and the thermostat UI.

### Topology Summary:
* **`attacker`** (10.1.27.23): Attacker VM hosting BIND9 nameserver and attack web server.
* **`local-dns`** (10.1.26.10): Local DNS server forwarding queries for `attacker32.com`.
* **`victim-iot`** (10.1.26.4): Protected internal machine running the IoT Thermostat server on port 8080 and Firefox browser.
levels.local_content: Submit the answer **start** to begin the training.

levels.title: Task 1: DNS Architecture & Zone Verification
levels.content:
Before conducting the attack, you must verify the DNS infrastructure. The attacker controls the domain `attacker32.com`. The **`attacker`** VM (10.1.27.23) acts as the authoritative nameserver for this domain. The **`local-dns`** server (10.1.26.10) has been configured with a forward zone for `attacker32.com` pointing to the attacker nameserver.

Your task is to verify that the local DNS server correctly forwards queries to the attacker's nameserver and retrieve the verification flag stored as a `TXT` record for `flag.attacker32.com`.

The flag is the text string contained in the `TXT` record of `flag.attacker32.com`.
levels.solution:
```bash
user@attacker:~$ dig @10.1.26.10 TXT flag.attacker32.com +short
```

The flag is: ${ANSWER}

hints.title: DNS Query Type for Verification
hints.content: Use the `TXT` record type with the `dig` command to query text records from the DNS server.

hints.title: Exact dig command syntax
hints.content: Run `dig @10.1.26.10 TXT flag.attacker32.com` from the command line. The response section contains the verification flag.

levels.title: Task 2: IoT Device & Same-Origin Policy Analysis
levels.content:
On **`victim-iot`** (10.1.26.4), the IoT thermostat server runs on port 8080 (`http://www.seedIoT32.com:8080`). It provides two APIs:
1. `/password`: returns a secret token required to authenticate temperature adjustments (anti-CSRF protection).
2. `/temperature`: receives target temperature and the password.

Open Firefox on **`victim-iot`** and browse to `http://www.attacker32.com:8080/change`. Click the "Click" button and open the Web Developer Console (F12 or `Tools -> Web Developer -> Web Console`). Notice that the request fails with a **Same-Origin Policy (SOP)** error because a script loaded from origin `http://www.attacker32.com:8080` is forbidden from reading data from origin `http://www.seedIoT32.com:8080`.

To complete this level, inspect the IoT device diagnostics at `http://www.seedIoT32.com:8080/info` (or via `curl http://10.1.26.4:8080/info` on `victim-iot`) to retrieve the Device Diagnostic Security Flag.
levels.solution:
```bash
# On victim-iot:
curl -s http://10.1.26.4:8080/info
```

The flag is: ${ANSWER}

hints.title: Understanding the SOP Restriction
hints.content: The Same-Origin Policy isolates origins defined by (protocol, host, port). Because `www.attacker32.com` does not match `www.seedIoT32.com`, the browser blocks the script from reading `/password`.

hints.title: Retrieving the Diagnostic Flag
hints.content: Browse to `http://www.seedIoT32.com:8080/info` on the victim machine or run `curl http://10.1.26.4:8080/info | jq` from the internal network.

levels.title: Task 3: Defeating SOP via Manual DNS Rebinding
levels.content:
Now defeat the Same-Origin Policy protection using **DNS Rebinding**:

### Step 1: Modify Malicious JavaScript
On the **`attacker`** VM, edit the JavaScript file `/var/www/rebind_malware/templates/js/change.js` (or `/home/seed/rebind_malware/templates/js/change.js`).
Change the first line from:
```javascript
let url_prefix = 'http://www.seediot32.com:8080'
```
to:
```javascript
let url_prefix = 'http://www.attacker32.com:8080'
```
Now the JavaScript makes requests to its own origin (`http://www.attacker32.com:8080`), complying with the SOP!

### Step 2: Remap the Domain (DNS Rebinding)
Edit the zone file `/etc/bind/zone_attacker32.com` on the **`attacker`** VM. Remap `www.attacker32.com` from `10.1.27.23` to the IoT server's IP address **`10.1.26.4`**.

### Step 3: Reload BIND9
Reload BIND9 so it serves the new mapping:
```bash
sudo rndc reload attacker32.com
```

### Step 4: Trigger the Payload on Victim
On **`victim-iot`**, wait 10 seconds for the Firefox DNS cache to expire. Then go to `http://www.attacker32.com:8080/change` and click the button.
The browser re-resolves `www.attacker32.com` to `10.1.26.4`. The AJAX request reaches the internal IoT thermostat and raises its temperature to **99°C**!

The flag is the confirmation token released by the IoT server once temperature reaches 99°C.
levels.solution:
```bash
# 1. On attacker VM, update /var/www/rebind_malware/templates/js/change.js:
# let url_prefix = 'http://www.attacker32.com:8080'

# 2. In /etc/bind/zone_attacker32.com, update www record to:
# www IN A 10.1.26.4

# 3. Reload BIND9:
sudo rndc reload attacker32.com

# 4. On victim VM, wait 10s and click 'Click' at http://www.attacker32.com:8080/change
```

The flag is: ${ANSWER}

hints.title: Aligning Request Target in change.js
hints.content: Since the page is served from `www.attacker32.com:8080`, the script must make requests to `http://www.attacker32.com:8080`. Update the `url_prefix` variable accordingly.

hints.title: Zone Modification and DNS Cache Expiration
hints.content: Replace the `A` record for `www` in `/etc/bind/zone_attacker32.com` with `10.1.26.4`. Run `sudo rndc reload attacker32.com`. You must wait at least 10 seconds (the Firefox cache expiration configured in Task 1) before clicking the button.

levels.title: Task 4: Automated DNS Rebinding Attack
levels.content:
In real attacks, attackers do not rely on victims manually clicking buttons at the exact right moment. In this task, you execute an **automated attack** against the IoT thermostat.

The automated payload is hosted on the attacker web server at `http://www.attacker32.com:8080/`. When the victim opens this page, a JavaScript timer counts down from 10 to 0. When it hits 0, it automatically fetches `/password` and sends a POST request to set the thermostat to a critical **88°C**.

### Attack Procedure:
1. Reset the `www` DNS record in `/etc/bind/zone_attacker32.com` back to `10.1.27.23` and reload BIND (`sudo rndc reload attacker32.com`).
2. Open `http://www.attacker32.com:8080/` in Firefox on **`victim-iot`**. The timer begins counting down from 10.
3. While the countdown is running, switch the `www` DNS record in the zone file to point to the IoT server (`10.1.26.4`) and run `sudo rndc reload attacker32.com`.
4. When the countdown reaches 0, the browser's DNS cache expires. The browser queries the DNS server, gets `10.1.26.4`, and silently pushes the exploit request to the internal thermostat!
5. Check the thermostat thermometer at `http://www.seedIoT32.com:8080/`. It will display the critical 88°C overheat state along with your Final Flag!

The flag is the Critical Overheat Flag displayed on the thermostat interface.
levels.solution:
```bash
# 1. Point www back to attacker: www IN A 10.1.27.23
sudo rndc reload attacker32.com

# 2. Open http://www.attacker32.com:8080 on victim-iot.

# 3. During countdown, change www IN A to 10.1.26.4 and reload:
sudo rndc reload attacker32.com

# 4. Timer hits 0 -> thermostat reaches 88°C!
```

The flag is: ${ANSWER}

hints.title: Automated Rebinding Timing and Sequence
hints.content: The victim must first load the attack page from the attacker VM (10.1.27.23). Once the page is loaded, update the zone file to point `www` to `10.1.26.4` and run `sudo rndc reload attacker32.com` before the timer expires.

hints.title: Verifying Critical Temperature Threshold
hints.content: Observe the thermometer at `http://www.seedIoT32.com:8080/` on victim-iot. Once temperature equals 88°C, the overheat alert reveals the final flag. You can also view it by running `curl http://10.1.26.4:8080/flag` on victim-iot.
